items.prose: Large insurance losses $X$, in £m, have density $f(x) = \tfrac{2}{x^3}$ for $x \ge 1$.
items.question: What is $E[X]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $x f(x) = \tfrac{2}{x^2}$ from 1 to infinity.

byKey.area: 1 is the total area, $\int f$. Multiply by $x$ first.
byKey.half: You integrated $\tfrac{2}{x^3}$ times $\tfrac{1}{x}$. Multiply by $x$, giving $\tfrac{2}{x^2}$.

explain.text: $x f(x) = \tfrac{2}{x^2}$, and $\left[-\tfrac2x\right]_1^\infty = 0 + 2 = 2$. The mean is finite, but $E[X^2] = \int_1^\infty \tfrac2x\,dx$ is infinite: a fat tail.

items.prose: A lognormal price has its mean 10% above its median.
items.question: What is $\sigma$, the sd of the log price? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean over the median is $e^{\sigma^2/2}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}}{e^{\mu}} = e^{\sigma^2/2} = 1.1$, so $\sigma^2 = 2\ln 1.1 \approx 0.1906$ and $\sigma \approx 0.4366$. The gap between mean and median measures the volatility.

items.question: What is the daily sd? Give it in %.

items.prose: A £100 share has drift $m = 8\%$ and volatility $\sigma = 30\%$ a year, in the lognormal model.
items.question: What is the chance it is below £100 after 2 years? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The log drifts by $(m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2})T$ and has sd $\sigma\sqrt T$.

byKey.no-drag: You used $mT = 0.16$ as the log drift. Subtract $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}T = 0.09$ first.
byKey.no-root: You used $\sigma T = 0.6$ as the log sd. Over 2 years it is $\sigma\sqrt2 \approx 0.4243$.
byKey.half: The log drift is positive, $0.07$, so a fall is less likely than a rise.

explain.text: Over 2 years the log drifts by $(0.08 - 0.045) \times 2 = 0.07$ with sd $0.3\sqrt2 \approx 0.4243$. So $P(S_2 < 100) = \Phi\left(\tfrac{-0.07}{0.4243}\right) = \Phi(-0.165) \approx 0.4345$.
